title: Stock Exchange
oneLine: Keep the trading critical path deterministic and single-writer per symbol partition: gateway, pre-trade risk, sequencer, in-memory matching engine, ordered fills, then asynchronous market data and reporting.
opening: I would divide the exchange into a latency-critical trading path and asynchronous market-data/reporting paths. Brokers connect through lightweight gateways—FIX or a proprietary low-latency protocol. The order manager authenticates, applies pre-trade risk and funds reservation, then sends a minimal command to a sequencer. Each symbol belongs to one matching-engine partition with a single ordered input stream, producing deterministic fills using price-time priority. The order book is in memory: ordered price levels, FIFO linked lists at each level, and an order-ID map for O(1) cancellation. Accepted commands and fills are written to a replicated event log so a hot standby can replay exactly. Market-data publishers rebuild books/candles from fills and distribute fairly, while reporting, surveillance, settlement, and analytics stay off the critical path. For microsecond-class latency, use pinned event loops, preallocated ring buffers, no blocking I/O/GC on the core, and colocated warm replicas with tested failover.
ask: Which instruments and order types—limit, market, cancel, replace?
Symbols, orders/day, peak at open, and latency percentile target?
What pre-trade risk, balance/position reservation, and regulatory checks?
Market-data depth, fairness, persistence, and recovery requirements?
scale: 1B orders over 6.5 trading hours is about 43K/s average and roughly 200K+/s at a 5× open peak.
Ordering is per symbol/partition, so scale by assigning symbols to matching cores while isolating exceptionally hot symbols.
Tail latency and jitter matter more than average; measure p99.9/p99.99 and pause sources such as GC, page faults, and network queues.

decisions.default: Single writer/event loop per symbol partition.
decisions.why: It eliminates locks and makes matching deterministic; parallelism comes from independent partitions.
decisions.switch: Do not parallelize one order book unless you can prove identical price-time outcomes.

decisions.default: Assign monotonic sequence to every accepted command and fill before state transition/publication.
decisions.why: It gives fairness, gap detection, replay, dedupe, and deterministic standby state.
decisions.switch: General Kafka may be acceptable for millisecond systems; specialized in-memory/WAL sequencing for microseconds.

decisions.default: Replicate ordered events to warm standby with a defined ACK point and zero-loss target.
decisions.why: A fill cannot disappear, but synchronous remote-region consensus may violate latency.
decisions.switch: Local synchronous replica plus asynchronous disaster-recovery region, with clear RPO/market halt policy.

decisions.default: Pre-trade hard limits and funds/position reservation before matching; complex surveillance after trade.
decisions.why: Only checks required to prevent invalid execution belong on the critical path.
decisions.switch: Cache/precompute risk state and make updates sequenced so the check remains deterministic.

decisions.default: Derive from the same ordered event stream and distribute via fair multicast/retransmission channels.
decisions.why: Subscribers should see a consistent book and no participant should gain accidental timing advantage.
decisions.switch: Internet clients consume normalized WebSocket/REST through a separate distribution tier.

deepDives.title: Order book
points: Buy side ordered highest price first; sell side lowest first.
Each price level holds FIFO orders for price-time priority; order-ID map points directly to linked-list node for O(1) cancel.
Partial fills update remaining quantity and may emit multiple executions.

deepDives.title: Low-latency mechanics
points: Pin event loop to CPU, preallocate objects/ring buffers, avoid locks, blocking calls, allocation, and synchronous logging.
Use memory-mapped/shared-memory queues within a host and carefully designed kernel-bypass/UDP where warranted.
Keep the core small; move enrichment, persistence views, and reporting off-path.

deepDives.title: Deterministic recovery
points: Standby consumes identical sequenced commands but is fenced from publishing.
Snapshots accelerate replay; event log remains authoritative for the gap.
Compare sequence/checksum before promotion and prevent split brain through lease/fencing/market-halt rules.

deepDives.title: Fair market data
points: Publish one canonical ordered feed; sequence packets and support gap requests/retransmission.
Multicast reduces distribution skew inside controlled networks but UDP loss must be repaired.
Colocation rules, timestamping, and capacity allocation require governance, not only technology.

deepDives.title: Capital-markets connection
points: Relate gateway/entitlement/risk boundaries to trader-facing APIs and OpenFin workflows.
Separate authoritative order/fill state from UI blotters and derived market data.
Discuss idempotent order commands, sequence gaps, partial fills, cancels, and stale-position risk using concrete desk experience.

failures.response: Fence old leader, promote validated warm standby at known sequence, replay gap, and halt/reject if determinism cannot be proven.
Client order ID/idempotency plus session/sequence; return existing state rather than enqueueing twice.

failures.risk: Gap in inbound or market-data sequence
failures.response: Stop processing beyond the gap, request replay/retransmission, and never silently reorder.
Sequence reservations/updates with orders, conservative reject on uncertain hard limits, and reconcile positions/funds after fills.
Dedicated core/hardware, optimize/batch surrounding work, product throttles; one book’s strict order remains serial.

questions.q: Why not make the matching engine a set of microservices?
questions.a: The core needs deterministic sequential state transitions and ultra-low jitter. Networked services and distributed locks add latency and nondeterminism. Keep the core cohesive; scale by symbol partitions and isolate noncritical functions.
Choose the best opposing price, then consume orders FIFO within that price level. A tree/map locates best levels; linked lists preserve arrival order; an ID map enables cancellation.

questions.q: How do you achieve exactly-once fills?
questions.a: Sequence commands, make matching deterministic, persist/replicate the event log, identify every fill, and make downstream consumers idempotent. On retry/replay, the same sequence produces the same fill IDs/state.

questions.q: How do you fail over without split brain?
questions.a: Fencing token/leadership lease, known committed sequence, standby checksum/replay, gateway reroute, and a market-halt safety state when ownership is ambiguous. Availability never overrides market integrity.

questions.q: How would you explain this from your experience?
questions.a: Anchor on order lifecycle and trader UI: entitlements and validation at entry, idempotent command IDs, authoritative ordered state, partial-fill/cancel events, position/risk updates, and blotters as projections. Then distinguish your UI/API experience from the matching core while showing you understand both.

mistakes: Putting logging/database calls on the matching critical path
Claiming global horizontal scale for one order book
Ignoring partial fills and cancel races
Using wall-clock timestamps as the only ordering mechanism
Failing over without fencing and sequence proof
seniorSignal: This is an excellent case for you: emphasize deterministic ordered state, projection-based trader UIs, entitlement/risk boundaries, partial failure, and p99.99 latency. Integrity and fairness beat generic cloud patterns.
implementation: FIX/client gateways and a minimal binary internal protocol
Single-threaded Java/C++ matching core with preallocated price-level/order structures
Chronicle Queue/Aeron-style sequenced event transport or specialized replicated WAL
Warm standby, snapshots/replay, KDB+/columnar market-data analytics, and async reporter/surveillance
